Choose the Nelson-Siegel Decay from the Curvature Peak

Source: R/ns-loadings.R
ns_lambda.Rd

Converts between the decay parameter lambda and the maturity at which the curvature loading peaks. ns_lambda() goes from a maturity to a lambda; ns_curvature_peak() goes back.

Usage

ns_lambda(peak_maturity)

ns_curvature_peak(lambda)

Arguments

peak_maturity

Numeric. The maturity at which the curvature loading should peak, in whatever units the maturities are measured in.

lambda

Numeric. A decay parameter, per unit of maturity.

Value

A numeric vector of the same length as the input: ns_lambda() returns decays, ns_curvature_peak() maturities.

Details

The curvature loading $$L_3(m) = \frac{1-e^{-\lambda m}}{\lambda m} - e^{-\lambda m}$$ is maximised where \(\lambda m = 1.793282\), the root of \(\partial L_3 / \partial m = 0\). So one defensible way to pick lambda is to decide where the hump belongs and divide.

The point of doing it this way is units. Lambda is per unit of maturity, so its numerical value depends on whether maturities are years or months, and nothing about a lambda on its own says which. Stating a maturity instead settles it: ns_lambda(30) on a curve measured in months and ns_lambda(2.5) on the same curve measured in years describe the same shape.

That also explains why this package does not use Diebold and Li's 0.0609 as its default. That is the value they published for maturities in months, where it places the hump at 29.4 months. The functions here take maturities in years, so the same number places it at 29.4 years – off the end of most curves, where the slope loading is nearly parallel to the level loading and the two factors are not separately identified. ns_curvature_peak() reports that directly, and the package default is written as ns_lambda(3.5) instead.

Two cautions. The peak is flat – at half or double the nominal peak maturity the loading is still about 85 percent of its maximum – so lambda is not tightly determined by this choice, and the apparent precision of the result is misleading. And lambda sets the slope loading's decay at the same time, which is often the more consequential effect: a hump at 2.5 years leaves the slope loading at 0.53 by two years, while a hump at 10 years leaves it at 0.84. Where lambda can be estimated rather than chosen, for instance with fit_ns_model(method = "profile"), estimating it is usually better. Fixing it is still the right move for a panel, where the factors have to be comparable across dates.

See also

plot_dns_loadings to see the loadings a lambda produces, and fit_ns_model to estimate one instead.

Examples

# A hump at two and a half years, for maturities measured in years
ns_lambda(2.5)
#> [1] 0.7173128

# Diebold and Li aimed for a hump at 30 months, measuring maturities in
# months. That criterion gives 0.0598; the value they published, 0.0609,
# peaks a little short of it.
ns_lambda(30)
#> [1] 0.05977607
ns_curvature_peak(0.0609)
#> [1] 29.44634

# What the package default implies when maturities are in years
ns_curvature_peak(0.0609)
#> [1] 29.44634

# They are inverses
ns_curvature_peak(ns_lambda(4))
#> [1] 4
